title: None touch it but the purified
hookLine: a noble Qur'an in a guarded book, touched only by the purified (56:77–79)
tomorrow: He is with you wherever you are

lines: THE HIGHEST SHELF, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.
WASH FIRST, THEN TAKE IT DOWN.
cards: Walk into many Muslim homes and you'll find the Qur'an on the highest shelf, often wrapped in cloth, nothing stacked on top. When someone takes it down, they may pause, go and wash, and come back.
Children learn not to put it on the floor. A guest might be surprised by all the care around one book.
Much of it traces back to three verses near the end of Surah Al-Waqi'ah, and what those verses mean, Muslim scholars have discussed, with more than one answer, for a very long time.

teach.h: A NOBLE QUR'AN, A BOOK KEPT HIDDEN.
teach.b: Verses seventy-seven to seventy-nine. Pickthall: "That (this) is indeed a noble Qur'an In a Book kept hidden Which none toucheth save the purified". Three things.
The Qur'an is karim, noble, generous. It is in a kitab maknun, a book kept hidden, guarded. And none touches it but the mutahharun, the purified.
Many classical commentators said the hidden book is the heavenly original, the preserved tablet, and the purified who touch it are the angels.
On that reading, the verse describes the Qur'an's source, not a rule for people. Others read it as also pointing to the written copy on earth, the mushaf.
And most jurists, whichever reading they held, required ritual purity to touch the mushaf.
They leaned as well on a letter the Prophet ﷺ sent to 'Amr ibn Hazm in Yemen, preserved in Malik's Muwatta: none should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure.
So the four main Sunni schools, and Shia jurists too, generally hold that you should be in wudu, the washing before prayer, to touch the written Arabic text.
A minority of scholars, among them Ibn Hazm of Andalusia, didn't require it. Reciting from memory without wudu is widely allowed.
Whatever the ruling, the habit it built is the one in the hook: the book isn't just picked up. It's prepared for.
The washing comes first, and the reading after.

how: Most Muslims make wudu before touching the Arabic mushaf, keep it in a high, clean place, and often wrap it in cloth; reciting from memory without wudu is widely permitted, and schools differ on details.

o: the scholars who memorized every verse
the purified, who alone touch the guarded book
the water used for washing before prayer

games.q: three verses in Al-Waqi'ah — tap the pairs.

s: every commentator reads 'the purified' as people in wudu
many classical commentators said the purified are the angels.
most jurists require wudu to touch the mushaf
the main Sunni schools and Shia jurists generally require it.
reciting from memory always requires wudu
reciting from memory without wudu is widely allowed.

games.q: you want to read from the Arabic mushaf but you're not in wudu. what do most schools of law say?
o: make wudu first, then touch it.
games.why: most jurists required ritual purity to touch the mushaf, citing this verse and the Prophet's letter to 'Amr ibn Hazm; a minority, like Ibn Hazm, did not.

practice: If you're Muslim, you might make wudu now, slowly, noticing the water on hands, mouth, face, arms, head and feet, then sit before you open the Qur'an.
If that isn't yours, wash your hands and face slowly, with full attention, and come back to sit before whatever you read next. Let the water be the beginning of the reading.

wordCard.voice: Mutahharun: the purified, those alone said to touch the guarded book that holds a noble Qur'an, honored on earth with wudu. Today's word.
